For months now, Werner has dedicated his every waking moment to this contraption. It has not been an easy journey. His stomach rumbled, the pain almost unbearable. How long had it been since his last meal? He wasn’t sure, maybe yesterday, perhaps. Perhaps the day before that. None of it mattered, now that he was done. Werner took long strides charged with purpose and anticipation over to his laptop. The screen left a soft reflection on his glasses, of a black background with green text, the code, the program, that made everything possible. A sequence of numbers, his final piece of the puzzle.

To the left of his laptop sat a picture of a woman and a young girl, both smiling. Both possessing pretty, warm, welcoming smiles splayed across their faces. Brown hair ever so slightly perturbed by a gentle breeze. Green eyes glistening in the sunlight, looking into the camera with a love that was reserved for a father, a husband. What would his wife think of what he had become? He knew she wouldn’t recognize him, would be repulsed by him. The sight of his daughter made his chest hurt, and a lump rose in his throat that threatened to choke the life from him. He wished it would. Too much. Need to focus, get it done.

Werner uploaded the code to a phone, his laptop closed with an audible click. He left it where it sat, he didn’t need it now, he was confident it would work. Tests and first drafts were for losers and morons, and Werner was neither. With a firm tug, the sync cable fell free from his machine. Hidden inside the contraption was just enough homemade Semtex to kill a man, if it were detonated close enough. He had to gett it close enough.

His target was held in a maximum security prison, locked away behind a small army of guards. Muhammad Abedi had murdered Werner’s family while they were on their way home to him. His girls were walking to their car when Muhammad detonated the bomb he’d planted outside of a children’s show. Werner’s family wasn’t even attending the show, they just happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time. Angela, Werner’s wife, had been on the phone with him when it happened.

A piercing shrill broke the silence, his alarm telling him to go to work. Werner added the final touch to his contraption, and headed for his car. He had a stop to make on his way to work. At the corner of destiny and fate, he flung the contraption from his car. The metaphorical bullet had left the chamber, there was no going back now. The sequence of numbers on his laptop, GPS coordinates, guided his fatal contraption home.

Now at work, Werner punched in and made his rounds. His heart was racing, palms covered in sweat, stomach a roiling broth begging to be expelled. The sound of dozens of inmates talking nearly hid the crisp sound of his boots striking the cheap tile floor. He reached Mohammad’s cell, and stuck his hand through the bars, a smart phone in his grasp. With a curious look, Mohammad took the phone from him, and the screen lit up. On it, a video, a stream from beyond the world of prison. Werner’s fatal contraption, merely a sophisticated child’s toy, was a remote controlled car with GPS guidance added to it. The numbers from Werner’s laptop were the coordinates for Mohammad’s home. The final touch, a note written atop the toy saying, “To Omar, love daddy.”

Werner watched with a smile, as Mohammad watched his son’s head evaporate into a cloud of red mist. With a clang and a bump, the phone fell to the floor, Werner’s program quietly and quickly erasing every trace, ensuring that he would go uncaught. It was far too soon for Werner to get caught, he had so much more vengeance left to give.
